title: Moon sighting debates
hookLine: calculation or sighting, local or global, still debated
tomorrow: Prayer times in the far north

cards: It's the twenty-ninth night of Ramadan, and the family group chat is busy. One mosque has announced: Eid is tomorrow. Another, across town, says: not yet, we fast one more day.
An aunt forwards a sighting from another country. A cousin posts an astronomy chart. Somebody asks, half joking, whether the family is allowed two Eids.
Nobody is being careless. Every one of them is trying to start the feast on the right day.

teach.b: Begin with the Qur'an. People asked the Prophet about the new moons, and the answer, in Pickthall's translation, is: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage."
The moon is the calendar, but the verse doesn't say how to read it. That comes from the hadith.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: fast when you see it, end the fast when you see it, and if it is hidden from you, complete thirty days.
In another report he says his community does not write or calculate, and the month is sometimes this long and sometimes that, shown with his hands. Here's the first debate.
Some scholars read these words as a command: the month begins with a human eye seeing the crescent.
Others read the mention of not calculating as a description of that time, and accept astronomical calculation now that it can be done. The second debate has a story.
Imam Muslim records that a man named Kurayb was in Syria at the start of Ramadan, where they saw the new moon on Friday night.
Back in Medina he told Ibn 'Abbas, who said: we saw it on Saturday night, and we'll keep fasting until we complete thirty or see it ourselves. Isn't the sighting in Syria enough? Kurayb asked.
No, said Ibn 'Abbas; this is how the Messenger of Allah commanded us. So some communities follow a local sighting.
Others accept a sighting from anywhere, so one sighting starts the month for everyone.
Each can point to something in the sources. None of them is ignoring the moon.

how: Muslim communities decide the start of Ramadan and the Eids in different ways: some wait for a local sighting of the crescent, some accept a sighting from another country, and some follow astronomical calculation.

o: disputes over which country may announce the start of Hajj
arguments over whether the moon matters at all for the calendar
how Muslims differ on when a month begins: by eye, or by calculation

s: the Qur'an spells out exactly how to sight the moon
2:189 calls the new moons fixed seasons; the method comes from the hadith and how scholars read it.
in Sahih Muslim, Ibn 'Abbas did not follow the sighting from Syria
he told Kurayb they would fast until they completed thirty or saw it themselves.
the hadith says that if the moon is hidden, complete thirty days
fast when you see it, end the fast when you see it, and if it's hidden, complete thirty.

games.q: you're Ibn 'Abbas in Medina. Kurayb arrives from Syria: they saw the new moon a night before you did. what do you do?
o: adopt the Syrian date at once.
keep to your own sighting and complete the month.
ask the astronomers to settle it.
games.why: he kept to Medina's sighting and said this is how the Messenger of Allah commanded them. some scholars build the case for local sighting on this report; others read it differently.

practice: Picture a thin crescent low over the horizon just after sunset, and the people looking for it: someone on a rooftop, someone with a telescope, someone reading a table of numbers, someone waiting for a call from abroad, all facing the same sky.
If any of them annoys you, notice it and let it go. If you pray, remember the people who will be fasting or feasting on a different day from you.

wordCard.voice: Moon sighting debates. Seeing with the eye or calculating, one local sighting or one for everyone: questions Muslims still weigh about when a month begins. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the new crescent moon; 2:189 uses its plural.

carryVoice: Your line: one moon, many views. Every one of them is looking at the same sky. Until tomorrow.
